claims.text: Accumulative roll bonding followed by moderate annealing produces a refined, partially recrystallized microstructure in an aluminum alloy.
The refined, partially recrystallized microstructure provides higher strength than the unprocessed state.
The processed aluminum alloy retains ductility relative to the unprocessed state.
Multiple passes of accumulative roll bonding impose severe plastic deformation.
A short, intermediate-temperature anneal after accumulative roll bonding promotes partial recrystallization.
Moderate annealing times limit excessive grain growth.
Severe plastic deformation followed by partial recrystallization forms ultrafine-grained regions.
Severe plastic deformation followed by partial recrystallization forms clean grain boundaries.
Dislocations generated or retained by the processing contribute to strengthening.
Minimizing grain growth helps preserve elevated yield strength.
Balancing dislocation strengthening and restricted grain growth preserves high elongation.
The combined processing can increase tensile strength by approximately 50% or more relative to baseline.
The combined processing can simultaneously improve ductility relative to baseline.
Excessively high annealing temperatures can cause grain coarsening.
Prolonged annealing can cause grain coarsening.
Annealing-induced grain coarsening can negate the mechanical advantage of the refined structure.
The optimum rolling reduction and annealing conditions have not been completely established.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as as-cast or solution-treated, while the hypothesis also allows comparison with an as-rolled state and the baseline is described only as unprocessed or as-cast. These non-equivalent starting and reference states make the intended control ambiguous.

The hypothesis is limited to suitably moderate, optimized processing conditions and explicitly predicts failure under excessive annealing, but the falsification rule says failure of any processed condition across varied strains, temperatures, and durations invalidates the hypothesis. Thus, an intentionally non-optimal condition would both be expected to fail and be treated as decisive falsification.
